title: The Fight

jokes.text: Sounds like you took a snake and twisted it like a rag until its blood and guts came out.
jokes.setup: Tom introduces his new product 'Snake Juice' with enthusiasm.
jokes.punchline: Ron responds with a grotesquely literal interpretation of the name, delivered in total deadpan.
jokes.explanation: Classic Ron Swanson deadpan. The joke works because it's hyper-literal, disgustingly specific, and completely in character — Ron has zero interest in salesmanship or social graces. 'Twisted like a rag' is a vivid and unexpected image. Strong character integration makes this more than a generic gross-out.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: It's a Kahlua-style liqueur. I call it Snake Juice.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Snake Juice? That sounds like... I don't even want to think about what that sounds like.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: What? It's just a name.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: It sounds like something you'd find at a rest stop bathroom.

jokes.text: What does Kahlua-style mean? / I mix a bunch of alcohol together, I add some sugar and coffee and some other junk, and it kind of tastes like Kahlua.
jokes.setup: Tom pitches Snake Juice as a 'high-end, Kahlua-style liqueur.'
jokes.punchline: His actual recipe is laughably slipshod — 'some other junk' and 'kind of tastes like Kahlua.'
jokes.explanation: The gap between Tom's grandiose branding language and his vague, careless recipe is a well-structured character joke. 'Some other junk' undercuts all pretension perfectly. Solidly earns its laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Kahlúa-style means it's got that smooth, sophisticated coffee liqueur vibe, you know? It's the kind of drink you serve at a fancy dinner party when you want people to think you have taste. Which I do. Obviously. It's basically just saying 'this is classy as hell.'

jokes.text: The 'Done-zo list' explanation — Tom elaborates: 'You want to come over to my house and play video games? Done-zo. Hey, Tom, you want to come play Putt-Putt with me? No, we're done-zo.'
jokes.setup: Tom threatens people with being on his 'Done-zo list' if they don't attend his meeting.
jokes.punchline: He is forced to laboriously explain what 'done-zo' means by playing both sides of hypothetical social scenarios, including Putt-Putt.
jokes.explanation: Tom's inability to read the room — the threat only works if people already understand the slang — is perfectly in character. The Putt-Putt example is a funny specific detail. The joke runs a bit long but the accumulation pays off.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: A Done-zo list? It's a comprehensive catalog of all the romantic prospects I've exhausted in this town. We're talking about women I've dated, women who've rejected me, women who've restraining-ordered me. It's color-coded, cross-referenced, and regularly updated.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: So when I'm looking to pursue someone new, I consult the Done-zo list to make sure I'm not wasting my time on someone who's already made it clear they'd rather see me hit by a bus.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Last week, I tried to ask out this woman at the grocery store, checked the list, and sure enough—she's on there. Turns out we went to mini golf together three years ago and I spent the whole time talking about my cryptocurrency portfolio while she was trying to break up with me.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: So no, we're done-zo. And I mean that literally—we got kicked out of Putt-Putt because apparently you can't re-propose to someone at the windmill hole when they've already said no twice.

jokes.text: I just... I couldn't deal with his face.
jokes.setup: Leslie and Ann discuss a recent breakup. Leslie says she liked the guy.
jokes.punchline: The reason for breaking up: 'I just couldn't deal with his face.'
jokes.explanation: Maximally economical. The casual delivery of a devastating and absurd reason is the joke. 'His face' as a dealbreaker stated with no further elaboration is brilliantly blunt. Short and lands cleanly.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: So why did you and Jesse break up?

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: He said he wanted to get back together with his ex-girlfriend.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh my God, that's terrible!

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Yeah, but honestly? I'm pretty sure I only dated him because he looked like a young Marlon Brando.

jokes.text: Oh, well, I'm technically out of the country. So I would have to call him from a weird number.
jokes.setup: Leslie asks if Ann can get a book back from her ex.
jokes.punchline: Ann explains she is 'technically out of the country' — an absurd diplomatic fiction — and would call from a 'weird number' to avoid being recognized.
jokes.explanation: The logic of being 'technically out of the country' is delightfully weird. The joke lands on absurd social avoidance behavior that's relatable but phrased in the most convoluted way possible.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I can't get it back. He's probably reading it right now, and if I interrupt him, I might startle him, and he could have a heart attack, and then I'd be responsible for his death.

jokes.text: She's gonna be up all night cramming... / She might be up all night, but I think someone else is gonna be doing the cramming.
jokes.setup: Leslie explains Ann will be up all night cramming for a job interview.
jokes.punchline: Jean-Ralphio immediately makes a sexual double entendre out of 'cramming.'
jokes.explanation: A fairly standard double entendre but elevated by Jean-Ralphio's specific energy and the 'Uh-oh!' tag. The joke is predictable but the delivery sells it. Not especially original as wordplay.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Mattias is such a great boyfriend. He's sensitive, he's thoughtful, he's incredibly attractive...

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: The only problem is astrologically he's a Gemini-Scorpio cusp, which makes absolutely no sense.

jokes.text: Jerry, you'll be playing a boring beer drinker. Your name will be Jerry.
jokes.setup: Tom assigns roles for the guerrilla marketing exercise, giving Ron the exciting alter ego 'Brian Thunder.'
jokes.punchline: Jerry's role and character name are just... Jerry. No alias, no excitement, just his own boring name.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional economy and character integration. The contrast between Ron's glamorous alias ('Brian Thunder') and Jerry getting literally his own name as his undercover persona is perfectly structured. Tom's contempt for Jerry is communicated without a single extra word. One of the tightest jokes in the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Alright everyone, listen up. We need guerrilla marketing for my business. I'm assigning roles.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Jerry, you're playing yourself.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Wait, what? I don't understand.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: It's perfect. Nobody knows who you are, nobody cares what you do. You're basically invisible. That's exactly the vibe we're going for.

jokes.text: The guerrilla marketing rehearsal — Ron reads 'I want this night to get K-razzy' / 'Ca-razy. Like crazy.'
jokes.setup: Ron is given a script with Tom's absurd phonetic spelling of 'crazy' as 'K-razzy.'
jokes.punchline: Ron reads it literally ('K-razzy'), Tom corrects him ('Ca-razy. Like crazy.'), and the entire exercise is already a disaster.
jokes.explanation: The comedy here is layered: Tom's written dialect is absurd, Ron reads it with perfect literal obliviousness, and Tom has to explain that 'crazy' means 'crazy.' The cringe builds on Ron's total incompatibility with Tom's world. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: It's K-razzy. With a K. It means crazy.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Why would you do that?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Because it's fun. It's a fun word. You just... you say it and it makes you feel good.

jokes.text: I won't publicly endorse a product unless I use it exclusively and I really believe in it. My only official recommendations are U.S. Army-issued mustache trimmers, Morton Salt, and the C.R. Laurence Fein two-inch, axe-style scraper oscillating knife blade.
jokes.setup: Tom asks Ron to endorse Snake Juice as part of the marketing exercise.
jokes.punchline: Ron has a very specific, very Ron list of endorsed products — culminating in an absurdly specific industrial knife blade.
jokes.explanation: This is elite character comedy. The specificity of Ron's endorsement list — Morton Salt is mundane, Army mustache trimmers are on-brand, but the precise model number of an oscillating knife blade is the escalating absurdist peak — perfectly encapsulates his character. The joke is funny, quotable, and tells you everything about Ron Swanson in three products. Justifies the high score.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I don't endorse products I don't believe in. But I do recommend a cast iron skillet, a good whiskey, and a solid handshake. Those are the only three things a man needs.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Well, that and a reliable axe. And a bench vise. And a quality wood stain.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: And perhaps some sandpaper. Various grits.

jokes.text: Short answer, he went bananas. Long answer, his wife Jan had an affair, gave him a venereal disease, and so he put signs about her all through City Hall.
jokes.setup: Ben explains why the PR Director was fired.
jokes.punchline: The 'long answer' to 'went bananas' is a cascade of increasingly awful events leading to public humiliation signage.
jokes.explanation: The 'short answer/long answer' framing is a clean structure that escalates well. The comedy is in the sheer accumulation of disaster and the clinical delivery of 'venereal disease' in a workplace briefing.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Dennis Cooper went completely bananas after his wife's affair. He started putting up these increasingly desperate and pathetic public signs all over City Hall.

jokes.text: The Jan Cooper signs — 'Chlamydia affects nearly 100% of Jan Coopers.' / 'The Department of Health congratulates Jan Cooper. Miss Chlamydia.' / 'Re-elect Jan Cooper. Mayor of Whoreville.'
jokes.setup: Dennis Cooper plastered City Hall with signs about his cheating wife.
jokes.punchline: The signs escalate from health warnings to a congratulatory crown to a political parody slogan — 'Mayor of Whoreville.'
jokes.explanation: Each sign is funnier than the last. The genius is that they're formatted as legitimate government health communications — 'Chlamydia affects nearly 100% of Jan Coopers' mimics CDC language perfectly. The final 'Mayor of Whoreville' is the comedic peak. Very well-structured escalation with genuine originality.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis Cooper
dialogue.line: I've had this STD for three years now. I call it my 'Miss Universe.'

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Why would you call it that?

dialogue.speaker: Dennis Cooper
dialogue.line: Because it's been around the world and it never goes away.

jokes.text: Leslie gives Ann the book 'Freedom by Jonathan Franzen' to read the night before a job interview. 'Because I'm almost done with it, Ann. And I want to talk to you about Patty.'
jokes.setup: Leslie has loaded Ann up with homework for the interview including energy drinks and espresso beans.
jokes.punchline: The inclusion of a lengthy literary novel is revealed to be entirely for Leslie's own benefit — she wants a book club partner.
jokes.explanation: This is a sharply observed moment of Leslie's character — her overwhelming helpfulness conceals a self-serving component delivered with total sincerity. 'I want to talk to you about Patty' as a casual aside is the perfect punchline.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Wow.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I know, right? 9 AM is pretty early, but I pulled some strings.

jokes.text: And let's be honest, it would be nice to not have to pull strange things out of people's butts every night. / It happened once. Just once. / That already is too many times.
jokes.setup: Leslie makes the case for Ann's career change, listing benefits including office hours.
jokes.punchline: The job perk of not extracting foreign objects from patients is introduced, disputed ('just once'), and immediately countered ('that is already too many times').
jokes.explanation: A perfectly three-beat joke. Setup, denial, absolute dismissal of the denial. 'That is already too many times' is the kind of deadpan line that gets rewound. The structure is tight and the escalation is efficient.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Because I assigned it. And I need to know if it's good so I can recommend it to people and they'll think I'm well-read and sophisticated.

jokes.text: Think about it as role-playing. / That makes it sexy. / That could be fun. / Can I use a weird voice and try to freak people out?
jokes.setup: Someone (likely Leslie) frames the guerrilla marketing as role-playing to motivate reluctant participants.
jokes.punchline: April's deadpan 'that makes it sexy' plus Andy's sincere enthusiasm for using a weird voice to freak people out.
jokes.explanation: April and Andy's relationship dynamic in miniature. April is darkly amused, Andy is sincerely excited about the strangest possible application. The juxtaposition of their two very different takes on the same premise works well.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I think about it every single day.

jokes.text: "Uh-oh, uh-oh. 'K' to the 'N' to the 'O-P-E,' she's the dopest little shorty in all Pawnee, Indiana."
jokes.setup: Jean-Ralphio greets Leslie at the club.
jokes.punchline: He breaks into a spontaneous rap — his standard greeting mode — spelling out 'KNOPE' and ending on 'Pawnee, Indiana,' which kills the rhythm entirely.
jokes.explanation: Jean-Ralphio's rapping is his signature move. The joke is the anti-climax of 'all Pawnee, Indiana' — the full state name kills any flow he had. Followed by Ben's deadpan 'Why didn't you just stop at Pawnee?' which is the better half of the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Come on, April! Let's do some role-playing to make this more fun!

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Okay. I'm a dead-eyed woman who has completely given up on life, and you're the reason why.

jokes.text: Why didn't you just stop at 'Pawnee'?
jokes.setup: Jean-Ralphio raps 'she's the dopest little shorty in all Pawnee, Indiana.'
jokes.punchline: Ben's calm, logical observation that 'Indiana' ruins the line.
jokes.explanation: Ben as the perpetual straight man works perfectly here. Maximum economy — six words that land the joke. His complete lack of excitement about Jean-Ralphio is consistent and funny.

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: Yo, yo, yo. Leslie Knope, she's so dope, she climbs a rope, like an antelope.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Jean-Ralphio, I appreciate the effort, but 'dope' and 'rope' rhyme, 'antelope' doesn't rhyme with those words. That's not how rhyme schemes work.

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: Nah, nah, nah, you're wrong. It's called a slant rhyme.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: It's called not knowing what you're talking about.

jokes.text: Ann shows up at the bar the night before her job interview. Leslie's reaction — the pause and 'Oh.'
jokes.setup: Leslie spent all evening preparing Ann for a 9am interview, including a stack of reading materials.
jokes.punchline: Ann is at the club instead. Leslie's 'Oh.' is an entire argument compressed into one syllable.
jokes.explanation: A great mockumentary reaction beat. The comedy is entirely in what Leslie doesn't say — the gap between her elaborate preparation and Ann's presence at a bar is the joke. Leslie's polite fury compressed into 'Oh.' is precisely observed.

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: Cramming? I'm great at cramming. One time I crammed so hard, I threw out my back.

jokes.text: Oh, well, there was way too much stuff for me to read tonight, anyway. I mean, it was a ridiculous amount of stuff that you gave me.
jokes.setup: Ann tries to explain why she's at the bar instead of studying.
jokes.punchline: She pivots from excuse-making to subtly complaining about how much work Leslie gave her — a defensive move that immediately antagonizes Leslie.
jokes.explanation: Functional cringe comedy — Ann making a bad situation worse by complaining about Leslie's help. Not brilliantly constructed but serves the scene's escalating tension.

dialogue.speaker: The Douche
dialogue.line: Hey ladies, are you a parking ticket? Because you've got FINE written all over you. Wait, that doesn't work. Are you from a parking lot? Because you're taking up two spaces in my heart.

jokes.text: Is there enough room for some 'man-aise' in this lady sandwich?
jokes.setup: Leslie and Ann are talking at the bar.
jokes.punchline: The Douche interrupts with one of the worst pickup lines conceivable, delivered with complete confidence.
jokes.explanation: The joke is that 'The Douche' is a perfect specimen of his type — the line is bad in exactly the right way to characterize him. 'Man-aise' is a genuinely weird coinage that makes the awfulness memorable.

dialogue.speaker: The Douche
dialogue.line: Oh my God, Leslie Knope! You listen to The Douche?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: No, I... I was just—

dialogue.speaker: The Douche
dialogue.line: You know what? You're gonna love this. Last week I did a whole segment called 'Eating Foods off a Stripper's Body.' It was my proudest moment as a radio personality.

jokes.text: Wait! Were you on the show where we had that stripper do math? Classic, right?
jokes.setup: Leslie mentions she was on The Douche's radio show once.
jokes.punchline: His only memory of guest segments is 'the one where a stripper did math' — an absurd premise he recalls with nostalgia.
jokes.explanation: A concise and effective bit of world-building. The specificity of 'a stripper doing math' is funny on its own, and that this is a memorable highlight of The Douche's radio career tells you everything about him and his audience.

dialogue.speaker: The Douche
dialogue.line: That was classic, right?

jokes.text: Leslie's silent reaction beat after The Douche asks about the stripper-math show — the camera presumably catches her expression.
jokes.setup: The Douche asks if she was on the stripper-math show.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's pause and non-answer — she clearly was, and is mortified, or she wasn't and is equally mortified by the question.
jokes.explanation: The beat after The Douche's question lands in silence and is part of the joke. Leslie's response (or non-response) is the punchline. Reaction beats in mockumentaries often earn their laughs from the cut or the expression.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Okay, so I'm a rogue intelligence agent who was disavowed by the government for knowing too much about Area 51.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: And I'm a washed-up stuntman trying to rebuild my reputation after a scandal involving a horse and a wedding cake.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: We meet in Budapest to distribute these flyers about a new frozen yogurt shop.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: But we can't let anyone know we're working together, because if the wrong people find out, they'll kill us both.

jokes.text: Hello, strange person who I have never met before. / Who are you? / I'm Janet Snakehole. I'm a very rich widow with a terrible secret.
jokes.setup: Andy approaches April at the club as promised — 'next time you see me, I'll be a stranger.'
jokes.punchline: April is playing a fully committed character: 'Janet Snakehole, a very rich widow with a terrible secret.' The bit is played completely straight.
jokes.explanation: Janet Snakehole is one of Parks and Rec's great recurring bits in miniature. 'A very rich widow with a terrible secret' delivered in complete earnestness is April at her best — utterly committed to a game that she controls. Perfectly in character and the start of an extended comic thread.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: April, you look like a snack. A very legal, consensual snack.

jokes.text: Bert Macklin, FBI. I was the best damn agent they had until I was framed for a crime I didn't commit. Stealing the President's rubies. Now I work alone.
jokes.setup: April/Janet Snakehole asks who Andy is.
jokes.punchline: Andy is playing 'Bert Macklin, FBI' — a fictional agent with a very specific crime he didn't commit: 'Stealing the President's rubies.'
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. 'Stealing the President's rubies' as the specific false charge is brilliantly absurd — it sounds exactly like something a child would invent. Andy's complete sincerity in delivering this is what makes it transcendent character comedy. 'Now I work alone' is the perfect capper. This is the kind of joke that gets remembered.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Ron, I've got a foolproof investment opportunity for you. It's called 'Rent-a-Swag.' You rent out swagger to people who need it for job interviews or first dates.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Tom, no.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Okay, okay, hear me out. What about 'Entertainment 720 Part 2: Electric Boogaloo'? We make it bigger, badder, more expensive.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: You're describing the same business.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: No, no, this time we also sell the boogaloo separately. It's a revenue stream. Or—or what about 'Treat Yo Self: The Airline'? Every seat is business class, and we just hand you money for no reason.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: You'd be bankrupt before takeoff.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: That's the beauty of it, Ron. Bankruptcy is just a fresh start, and I'd be a phoenix rising from the ashes. A phoenix made of debt and poor decisions, but a phoenix nonetheless.

jokes.text: I got to admit, I thought your costume would maybe be a little bit sluttier.
jokes.setup: April/Janet Snakehole is playing her character in the club.
jokes.punchline: Jean-Ralphio bluntly and absurdly critiques her character's costume, expecting more skin.
jokes.explanation: A decent Jean-Ralphio line — his oblivious sexism delivered casually. Not the sharpest joke but in character. April's 'How dare you?' staying in character as Janet Snakehole is actually the funnier beat.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Ron, I'm offering you a chance to try Snake Juice. If you don't like it, you have to do whatever I say for a week.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: What do I get if I do like it?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Uh... you get to keep drinking Snake Juice?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm in. When do I start taking orders from you?

jokes.text: Tom's business pitch list: 'Make a baby tuxedo clothing line. A department store with a guest list. White fur ear muffs for men. Contact lenses that display text messages. Invent a phone that smells good. Own a night club called Eclipse that's only open for one hour two times a year. Cover charge, $5,000.'
jokes.setup: Jean-Ralphio tells Ron that Tom has the best investment ideas he's ever heard.
jokes.punchline: The list of Tom's 'brilliant' ideas escalates from plausibly bad (baby tuxedos) to absurdly ambitious (Eclipse: open one hour, twice a year, $5,000 cover).
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best jokes. Each successive idea is funnier than the last, and the list works as a perfectly calibrated portrait of Tom Haverford's delusions. 'A phone that smells good' is the mid-list peak, but 'Eclipse — open one hour, two times a year, cover charge $5,000' is a genuine comic masterpiece of absurdist character writing. Justifies the high score because every item earns its place and the cumulative effect is bigger than the sum of parts.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: This is... surprisingly smooth. What's in this?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Snake Juice, baby. Premium ingredients.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I was wrong about you, Haverford. This is excellent.

jokes.text: If you like it, I'll talk it up all night. If you don't, I'll shave Jean-Ralphio's head. / Yeah, I'd like to see that. Hit me.
jokes.setup: Tom tries to get Ron to try Snake Juice by offering a meaningful incentive.
jokes.punchline: Ron's motivation to try it isn't the product but the possible chance to see Jean-Ralphio get his head shaved — and his immediate acquiescence.
jokes.explanation: Classic Ron Swanson — he's immune to marketing enthusiasm but immediately engaged by the prospect of mildly punishing Jean-Ralphio. 'Yeah, I'd like to see that. Hit me.' is perfectly economical and perfectly in character. The structure sets up two possible outcomes and immediately reveals which one Ron prefers.

dialogue.speaker: The Douche
dialogue.line: My pickup line is, 'Are you a douche? Because I'm a douchebag and we belong together.'

jokes.text: Damn, if that isn't delicious. / 'R' to the 'O' to the 'N'... I say Swanson's got swagger the size of a Big Ben clock.
jokes.setup: Ron tries Snake Juice and is genuinely won over.
jokes.punchline: Jean-Ralphio immediately launches a celebratory rap. Ron cuts him off: 'I know what I have to do. You had it at Ben. I know. I got it.'
jokes.explanation: Ron conceding the rap should've ended at 'Ben' because it rhymed is a funny moment of his unexpected engagement with the situation. The contrast of Ron Swanson caring about rap flow is amusing.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: So how long do you think this thing with The Douche is going to last?

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Oh, I'd say about two more weeks. Maybe three if he doesn't do anything too stupid.

dialogue.speaker: The Douche
dialogue.line: I'm sitting right here.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I know.

jokes.text: Ron tastes Snake Juice: 'Damn, if that isn't delicious.' — Ron Swanson, the man who refused to endorse anything, is immediately won over.
jokes.setup: Ron has been resistant to everything; there's a beat of tension as he tries it
jokes.punchline: He loves it immediately, no hedging — the man of impossible standards is defeated by a cocktail made of 'alcohol, sugar, coffee, and some other junk'
jokes.explanation: Payoff on the extended Ron/endorsement setup. The brevity of his capitulation — 'Damn, if that isn't delicious' with no further commentary — is perfectly Ron. The callback to his elaborate refusal to endorse things makes the surrender funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That hat is a disaster. That hat makes you look like a sad, confused pilgrim.

jokes.text: Dude, you got to end it on the rhyme. / I know what I have to do. You had it at 'Ben.'
jokes.setup: Jean-Ralphio's rap about Ron ends on 'Big Ben clock' instead of rhyming cleanly.
jokes.punchline: Ron — a man who has shown zero interest in rap — immediately and correctly identifies the structural flaw in Jean-Ralphio's verse.
jokes.explanation: The surprise of Ron having an opinion on rap craft — let alone being correct — is the joke. Very economical and a great subversion of expectation.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I, Ron Swanson, do hereby endorse Snake Juice. It is a beverage of considerable quality. The alcohol content is robust. The aftertaste is minimal, if present at all. I have consumed many bottles of this product, and I am still alive. I recommend Snake Juice to anyone who enjoys drinking alcohol, or who simply wishes to forget. It is available at most establishments that sell liquor. I give it my highest recommendation.

jokes.text: The Janet Snakehole/Bert Macklin scene: 'I've been everywhere, darling... My husband kept me in the finest clothes from Bergdorf Goodman.' / 'Freeze! FBI!' / 'I didn't kill anybody! And I didn't burn down the mill either. My sister did. But now she's been eaten by wolves!'
jokes.setup: April (as Janet Snakehole) is working the room in character. Andy (as Bert Macklin) confronts her.
jokes.punchline: April's character defense escalates: she didn't kill anyone, didn't burn the mill (a mill!), her sister did it, but the sister has been eaten by wolves. Each clause is more absurd than the last.
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's comedic high point. The escalation of Janet's alibi — murder, arson, blame-shifting to a sister, sister eaten by wolves — is perfectly paced and completely unhinged. 'But now she's been eaten by wolves!' is a genuinely great comedy line. April and Andy's total commitment to completely improvised nonsense is peak character writing. 'Nothing to see here' as the capper by a bystander is the cherry on top. Comparable in quality to anchor examples at 9+ level.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: It's got electrolytes, it's got vitamins, it's got potassium. It's basically like Gatorade, except it can literally kill you.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Why would you lead with that?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Because it's exciting!

jokes.text: Nothing to see here. [bystander reaction to Bert Macklin/Janet Snakehole scene]
jokes.setup: Andy and April have just staged a dramatic FBI confrontation in the middle of a nightclub.
jokes.punchline: Someone simply says 'Nothing to see here' — the classic bystander dismissal applied to this very much something-to-see situation.
jokes.explanation: A light button on the Bert Macklin scene. Works as punctuation but not especially original — 'nothing to see here' is a familiar formula.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: It's 140 proof. Snake Juice.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: That will kill you.

jokes.text: 'If you're looking for douches, they're in Aisle Me.' — The Douche's pickup line for meeting Ann.
jokes.setup: Ann asks how she and The Douche met.
jokes.punchline: His pickup line repurposes his own nickname as a store directory joke — 'they're in Aisle Me.'
jokes.explanation: Surprisingly clever for a character defined by his terribleness. The line works on two levels — it's a functional pun AND it demonstrates The Douche's self-aware use of his own reputation as currency. The economy is perfect. Genuinely impressive wordplay from the writers.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You know what? You've always been kind of a boring person.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Oh, that's rich coming from you. You're obsessed with yourself.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: At least I care about things! You just drift through life like some kind of... blonde ghost.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: A blonde ghost? Really? You're drunk and you're not even making sense anymore.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I make perfect sense. You know what your problem is? You have no opinions. You're just a yes-woman.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: And you're exhausting! Not everything is about Parks and Rec, Leslie. Not everything is about you being the best at your job.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well at least I have a job I care about! What do you do? Model? Give advice nobody asked for?

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: You know what? I'm done. We're not even friends right now.

jokes.text: I should've known better than to loan something to one of your boyfriends. They come and go so fast.
jokes.setup: Ann mentions she can't get the book back from her ex.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's casual aside about Ann's boyfriends cycling through rapidly — said in front of Ann's current boyfriend.
jokes.explanation: A good cringe moment — Leslie being thoughtlessly insensitive while The Douche is sitting right there. The setup and payoff ('Sitting right here') works cleanly.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay, I'm going to stay calm and rational about this.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You're a big stupid head! Yeah, that's right! A stupid, stupid head with a stupid face!

jokes.text: The Douche, sitting right there, responds to Ann saying 'He's dumb, but he's fun' about him: 'Thank you.'
jokes.setup: Ann is explaining to Leslie that she dates around to 'try on different hats.' She describes her current boyfriend as 'dumb, but fun.'
jokes.punchline: The Douche is sitting right there and responds only with 'Thank you' — completely unbothered by and apparently accepting of 'dumb.'
jokes.explanation: Perfect joke. 'Thank you' is the ideal response — he takes the compliment ('fun') and accepts the insult ('dumb') with zero defensiveness, which reveals everything about his character. The economy is extraordinary: two words deliver a complete character portrait. This is the kind of joke a great comedy writer's room produces — simple, character-specific, maximally efficient. Earns its high score.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay, so... so the thing about waffles is that they're just... they're just pancakes that went to the gym, you know? And I respect that. I respect that commitment. But here's the thing - and this is important - we need to talk about the raccoons. They're planning something. I can feel it. They're in the walls, and they're... they're unionizing. We need a permit for that. Actually, we need to STOP that. Or encourage it? I'm not... I'm not entirely sure anymore. But Ben - Ben would know. Ben knows everything. He's so smart. Have I mentioned that? Because he is. He's like a human calculator, but prettier. Much prettier. Anyway, the point is... what was the point? Oh! Treat yo' self! But like, treat the raccoons too, because they're part of the community, and we're all in this together, and I just... I just love this town so much.

jokes.text: Well, I don't know. He's dumb, but he's fun. / Thank you.
jokes.setup: Leslie suggests Ann's current relationship won't last. Ann defends the relationship.
jokes.punchline: Her defense is that he's 'dumb but fun' — said in front of him. He thanks her. The sincere 'Thank you' from someone who just heard himself called dumb is the joke.
jokes.explanation: The Douche saying 'Thank you' to being called dumb is a perfect character joke. His complete lack of offense, apparently satisfied with 'fun,' tells you everything. Great economy — two words do the work.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I'm like a... I'm like a human version of a Golden Retriever mixed with a... with a sandwich. And that sandwich is also a Golden Retriever. You know what I mean?

jokes.text: Well, this hat is an idiot. / Classic.
jokes.setup: Leslie uses a hat metaphor for dating around: 'you get to try on a bunch of different hats.'
jokes.punchline: Ann extends the metaphor: 'this hat is an idiot.' The Douche responds, 'Classic,' still not registering the insult.
jokes.explanation: The callback is stronger than the original setup. Ann applying the hat metaphor directly to The Douche while he nods approvingly is a great escalation of the running gag of his obliviousness.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: You know what they say about elephants—they never forget. And you know what else never forgets? Howard Stern. That guy remembers everything.

jokes.text: Hello. My name is Ron Swanson. In general, I try never to speak with people, but I have been drinking this Snake Juice thing, and it's damn good. You should buy it. / Son, you should know that my recommendation is essentially a guarantee. Drink this, now.
jokes.setup: Ron has been convinced to endorse Snake Juice and approaches strangers.
jokes.punchline: His 'endorsement' begins with a confession that he tries never to speak to people, followed by the most blunt hard-sell possible: 'Drink this, now.'
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best payoffs. Everything Ron said about never endorsing products unless he truly believes in them has come true, and his genuine enthusiasm emerges in the most Ron Swanson way possible: zero warmth, maximum authority. 'My recommendation is essentially a guarantee. Drink this, now.' is a great line. Justifies a high score — it rewards viewers who remembered his earlier speech.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I'm in the woods... I'm in the woods... everybody's got a soul except for Andy... I'm a goofy goober... yeah... I got no rhythm... I got no game... but I got heart... I'm gonna eat some... some pizza... some waffles... some eggs... some bacon... some toast... some cereal... some milk... some cheese... some bread... some butter... some jam... some peanut butter... some jelly... some hot dogs... some buns... some ketchup... some mustard... some mayonnaise...

jokes.text: It's 140 proof, which means it's 70% alcohol. But don't worry. There's plenty of caffeine in it to keep you awake. / I believe an ounce of that would literally kill me.
jokes.setup: Tom explains Snake Juice's specs to Chris, who is on a cleanse.
jokes.punchline: Chris, a man who runs marathons and drinks cayenne water, calmly states that one ounce of this drink would kill him.
jokes.explanation: Good character integration — Chris's health obsession and physical perfection make his measured assessment of the drink's lethality funnier. 'I believe an ounce of that would literally kill me' said without alarm is perfectly deadpan.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Where should we drive first?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Butt first.

jokes.text: You emailed everyone at City Hall and told them to come to a club that you own to buy alcohol that you invented.
jokes.setup: Tom has been using his City Hall position to promote his private business.
jokes.punchline: Chris's flat recitation of the facts makes the scheme sound even more obviously wrong than Tom realized.
jokes.explanation: Chris's deadpan enumeration of the conflict of interest is effective. The comedy is in how obvious the violation was and Tom's apparent surprise at being caught.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Why are we even here? I mean, really, why are any of us here? We're all just floating through space on a rock, pretending our jobs matter, pretending our lives have meaning. April, do you ever think about that? We're all going to die.

jokes.text: Jean-Ralphio rapping Chris's title: 'B to the O to the double S, do what he say, and you'll be successful.'
jokes.setup: Tom tries to manage the awkward situation with his boss Chris by having Jean-Ralphio improvise a flattering rap.
jokes.punchline: Jean-Ralphio delivers a surprisingly coherent and advice-giving rap about following your boss.
jokes.explanation: Jean-Ralphio's on-demand rapping about authority figures is very in character. The joke is partly that he does this unsolicited and partly that the content of the rap is genuinely sensible advice.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait, you ran a 5k while hungover?

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Yes, I woke up this morning and felt great, so I thought I'd get some exercise in.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Chris, you're literally vomiting right now.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: I know, but I'm doing it while running!

jokes.text: No offense, but maybe you think I'm going too fast 'cause you're going too slow with Ben. / No offense, but I'm going slow because I might lose my job.
jokes.setup: Ann and Leslie's earlier tension re-emerges; Ann implies Leslie's caution about Ben is an excuse.
jokes.punchline: The escalating 'no offense' chain — each subsequent 'no offense' introducing something more offensive.
jokes.explanation: The 'no offense' escalation is a familiar structure but executed with character-specific content. The chain culminating in 'Offense! That's rude. I'm gonna go dance.' is a satisfying button.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: When you make a burger, you start with the meat. Now, some people will tell you to grind it yourself, but I recommend just going to the butcher and having him do it. He'll grind it up real nice. Then you take that meat, and you form it into a patty. You want it to be about this thick. Not too thick, not too thin. Just right. Then you throw it on the grill. You hear that sizzle? That's the sound of a job well done.

jokes.text: Talking head: 'This is my first fight with Ann, and it's a doozy. But I believe that honest discussions between friends can lead to deeper intimacy. This is a watershed moment in our relationship, and it's important that we fight clean.' Cut to Leslie: 'You're stupid, and you're drunk and you're stupid.'
jokes.setup: Leslie's talking head articulates a thoughtful philosophy about constructive conflict.
jokes.punchline: Immediate cut to Leslie calling Ann 'stupid, and drunk and stupid' — the opposite of fighting clean.
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's best pure comedy construction. The mockumentary format is used perfectly — Leslie's aspirational talking head followed by immediate evidence of complete failure. 'You're stupid, and you're drunk and you're stupid' is the exact right amount of drunk-person repetition ('stupid' twice). The structure is textbook and flawlessly executed. This is among the best jokes in the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I have a hangover so bad, I can see sounds and hear colors. My liver filed for divorce. I'm pretty sure I'm currently being haunted by a bottle of tequila.

jokes.text: 'Everything isn't your fault all the time. Don't always make everything your fault.' / 'Good! It's not all my fault. I'm not the stupid jerk.' / 'I'm not the one who's being a stupid jerk right now.'
jokes.setup: Leslie and Ann are drunkenly arguing at the bar.
jokes.punchline: Their argument is so circular and irrational that neither can land a coherent point — each new sentence contradicts or escalates the last.
jokes.explanation: The drunk logic loop is well-observed — the argument escalates while making no progress. The comedy is in recognizing the pattern of drunk circular arguments.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: April, I'm so sorry.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: For what?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I don't know, but I feel like I owe you an apology too.

jokes.text: Cleanse subplot: 'Every time I cleanse, I can literally feel the toxins leaving my body.' / 'I've still got a full week to go before the broth stage.' / 'Pre-broth is an amazing stage. It's when you're most alert.'
jokes.setup: Cut to Chris and Donna discussing the cleanse amid the chaos of the drunk night.
jokes.punchline: The juxtaposition of their earnest wellness discussion against the backdrop of Snake Juice mayhem — plus the absurd granularity of 'the broth stage.'
jokes.explanation: The comedy is in the contrast — calm wellness talk while everyone around them is disintegrating. 'The broth stage' as a milestone is a good specific absurd detail.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ben, I'm so sorry. I feel terrible about what happened.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, what are you talking about? What did you do?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I... I'm not entirely sure, but I know I need to apologize for it.

jokes.text: Good. Someone needs to be alert tonight. This Snake Juice is basically rat poison. Everybody's wasted.
jokes.setup: Chris and Donna agree that pre-broth is the most alert stage.
jokes.punchline: Chris surveys the room and delivers a clinical assessment: 'This Snake Juice is basically rat poison. Everybody's wasted.'
jokes.explanation: Chris's serene omniscience about the disaster unfolding around him is funny. 'Rat poison' is a good hyperbole and 'everybody's wasted' delivered with calm observation rather than alarm is perfect Chris Traeger.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ben, I'm so sorry.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: For what?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I have no idea.

jokes.text: Drunk Tom talking head: 'You don't even know one thing. I didn't even say one thing. And then she asked me the whole thing, and I didn't even do it once. I'm like an elephant, okay? If I walk into a room, it's like, okay, he's in there.'
jokes.setup: Tom gives a talking-head confessional while extremely drunk.
jokes.punchline: His speech is completely incoherent — noun-free, logic-free, but delivered with total conviction, ending on the profound non-insight that if he walks into a room, he is in the room.
jokes.explanation: A brilliant mock-confessional. The talking head format makes the incoherence funnier — these are supposed to be reflective moments. Tom's drunk gravity ('I'm like an elephant, okay?') building to the tautological 'if I walk into a room, it's like, okay, he's in there' is genuinely great absurdist comedy. The complete confidence makes it.

dialogue.speaker: Kyle
dialogue.line: Wait, if he's Bert Macklin's brother, why does he have a different last name?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Kyle, you're asking too many questions. Just go with it.

jokes.text: Tom: 'Bababooey.'
jokes.setup: Tom has just finished his incoherent elephant speech.
jokes.punchline: 'Bababooey' — the famous Howard Stern radio call-in phrase — delivered as a complete non-sequitur conclusion to the speech, as if it's a logical endpoint.
jokes.explanation: A single word as the button on an incomprehensible speech. Maximum economy — 'Bababooey' punctuates the nonsense perfectly. Works because it adds nothing and therefore adds everything.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Oh, so you bought my shares? Well, I'm gonna buy YOUR shares. And then I'm gonna buy your shares back. And then I'm gonna tell everyone you smell like a old gym sock.

jokes.text: Turn this music down. / Farts and poop and love and stuff. / Macaroni salad.
jokes.setup: Presumably a drunk scene in the car/aftermath.
jokes.punchline: Ron demands quiet; someone (likely drunk Andy) offers 'Farts and poop and love and stuff' as a song lyric or thought, then 'Macaroni salad' as a non-sequitur.
jokes.explanation: Pure drunk absurdism. 'Farts and poop and love and stuff' has a poetic quality that's funny, and 'macaroni salad' as a follow-up is a good non-sequitur. Not high craft but earns the laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: Because I'm keeping my club shares, and if anyone has a problem with that, I will hurt them.

jokes.text: Tom's in the trunk. Jerry's on the roof.
jokes.setup: Everyone is piling into a car to leave the club.
jokes.punchline: Ann matter-of-factly reports the seating arrangements: Tom is in the trunk, Jerry is on the roof.
jokes.explanation: The casual delivery of an absurd situation — Tom in the trunk, Jerry on the roof — with zero commentary is the joke. Maximum economy. The visual implied (Jerry on the roof) plus Ann's complete non-reaction is very funny. Great deadpan.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Vin Diesel's career is the perfect business model. He started small, did what he was good at, and then slowly expanded into different markets. Fast and Furious, xXx, Riddick - he diversified his portfolio while maintaining his core brand identity.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: That's what I'm doing with Rambunctious. Start local, build a loyal base, then franchise the hell out of it. In five years, Vin Diesel's going to wish he had my business plan.

jokes.text: All right, where to first? / Your mother's butt.
jokes.setup: Ron, the most sober person, is driving the drunk group home.
jokes.punchline: Andy's answer to 'where to first' is 'your mother's butt' — a playground-level comeback delivered by a genuinely drunk adult.
jokes.explanation: The joke is that Andy's drunk contribution to navigation is a 'your mom' joke. Not highly crafted but Andy's childlike earnestness makes it land. The contrast with Ron's stoic driving is the real joke.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, why are you wearing a tuxedo?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I don't know. I woke up like this.

jokes.text: I'm so alone.
jokes.setup: Jerry is apparently on the roof of the car.
jokes.punchline: From the roof, Jerry quietly says 'I'm so alone.' — not a complaint about being on the roof, but an existential declaration.
jokes.explanation: One of the great Jerry jokes. 'I'm so alone' from the roof of a moving car, while everyone else is inside, delivered as quiet resignation rather than complaint, perfectly encapsulates Jerry's entire character. Maximum economy — three words that are both funny and almost sad. The fact that no one responds makes it funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Why are you wearing snow pants in April?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Because last night, drunk me made a lot of sense. She said, 'You know what? Global warming. We might not have snow next year. You better enjoy it while you can.' And sober me was like, 'That's... not terrible logic.'

jokes.text: If even one of you thinks about dry-heaving in my car, you're all walking home.
jokes.setup: Ron is driving the drunk group home in his car.
jokes.punchline: Ron's threat has a collective punishment clause — not just the dry-heaver, but everyone walks home.
jokes.explanation: Ron's authoritarianism applied to car sickness is funny. The specific threat of 'dry-heaving' (not even actual vomiting) triggering collective punishment is characteristic Ron logic.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Oh my god, I just realized something. Last night we were like a bad rom-com montage. We had wine, we talked about our feelings, we made a friendship pact... We literally did everything except montage it to an indie song.

jokes.text: I feel great. I ran five k this morning. / Really? / No, I threw up in the shower.
jokes.setup: The morning after, everyone is hungover. Ben claims to feel great.
jokes.punchline: Immediate deadpan reversal — 'No, I threw up in the shower.' The misdirection of 'Really?' before the reveal works perfectly.
jokes.explanation: Near-perfect joke construction. The setup is a confident claim, the 'Really?' beat gives the audience a moment to wonder, and 'No, I threw up in the shower' is the most efficient possible deflation. The 'shower' specific detail is the right touch. One of the tightest jokes in the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Okay, as a medical professional, I can tell you that Snake Juice is 50% maple syrup and 50% a mixture of various liqueurs that should never be combined. The sugar content alone could kill a horse.

jokes.text: I brought some burgers and fries. Eat up. The protein soaks up the sugar.
jokes.setup: Everyone is hungover. Ron arrives apparently unaffected.
jokes.punchline: Ron brings burgers and fries — his preferred solution to every problem — and delivers folk wisdom about protein and sugar with complete authority.
jokes.explanation: Ron's immunity to the chaos and his meat-based solutions are consistent. The nutritional advice ('protein soaks up the sugar') is charmingly wrong in a Ron way. Good character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: So what does Leslie actually feel?

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Oh, it's simple. She likes you. You like her. You're both being stubborn idiots about it.

jokes.text: First, you take the cow to the killing floor...
jokes.setup: Ron is apparently explaining where burgers come from to hungover colleagues who did not ask.
jokes.punchline: His description of the burger begins with 'First, you take the cow to the killing floor' — beginning at the very beginning, graphically.
jokes.explanation: Ron Swanson's total lack of squeamishness about where food comes from — especially to hungover people — is a perfect character beat. 'The killing floor' as an opening to a hangover cure story is darkly funny.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: So Ben likes Leslie, Leslie likes Ben, and you're both just going to sit around and pine for each other like it's high school?

jokes.text: Well, I am out of questions. Thank you. We will let you know. [Interview scene ending abruptly]
jokes.setup: Ben and Leslie are interviewing candidates for the PR Director position while catastrophically hungover.
jokes.punchline: Ben ends an interview in what appears to be the first few seconds — 'I am out of questions' implies they asked virtually nothing.
jokes.explanation: The comedy is implied — we can infer from 'I am out of questions' that this interview lasted roughly 30 seconds. Good cringe setup for the hangover sequence.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis Cooper
dialogue.line: Still obsessing over his personal problems

jokes.text: Then our heads will explode, and we will die.
jokes.setup: They are apparently describing something extremely unpleasant (probably the next interview candidate's description of a medical condition or health initiative).
jokes.punchline: Leslie's summary is 'then our heads will explode, and we will die' — her hangover assessment of the stakes.
jokes.explanation: A functional hangover hyperbole. Works in context but not a particularly original line.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I'm here for my interview.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Ann, why are you wearing a bathing suit?

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Oh, I thought this was a beach interview.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: It's not. Also, you're wearing two different shoes.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I know. I'm very prepared.

jokes.text: Say, thanks, chum. I'll get those papers delivered for you. / Whatever. / Post-haste.
jokes.setup: Andy is doing his job (apparently a shoe-shining/delivery role) with unusual period formality.
jokes.punchline: 'Post-haste' as a sincere closing to a mundane interaction is an Andy-specific form of absurd formality.
jokes.explanation: A small Andy bit. His use of 'post-haste' sincerely in a casual context is endearing absurdism. Not a big joke but consistent with his character.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: That's the perfect anti-marketing slogan for Tom's product.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: What? No it's not!

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: "Regret and Shame" — it really captures the essence of what you're selling.

jokes.text: The doctor says it's probably not serious, but it might be. / Oh, Kyle, please stop talking.
jokes.setup: Jerry (called Kyle here, a recurring name-confusion gag) begins sharing a health concern.
jokes.punchline: Donna immediately shuts him down: 'Oh, Kyle, please stop talking.'
jokes.explanation: Jerry being called the wrong name is a running gag. Donna's preemptive dismissal of what sounds like a genuine health concern is darkly funny and character-appropriate.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I'm gonna be sick.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh my God, do you want me to come with you?

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: That would actually be really nice.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay, let's go throw up together.

jokes.text: Why, isn't it Bert Macklin? / What are you doing here, and who is this sorry Charlie? / I'm Janet Snakehole. I demand answers, and I want them now.
jokes.setup: The Bert Macklin/Janet Snakehole game continues into the next day at City Hall.
jokes.punchline: They have apparently not dropped character since the night before — the bit is now happening in a professional workplace setting.
jokes.explanation: The joke escalates by transporting the absurd game to an inappropriate context. Their total commitment to the bit at work, while colleagues try to have a normal day, is a perfect running gag payoff. 'Who is this sorry Charlie?' is a genuinely funny Bert Macklin line.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: You know, I've been thinking a lot about what really matters in life. And I realized something profound.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: It's not about the perfect job, or the perfect house, or having everything figured out.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: It's about the people you love, and showing up for them every single day.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Which is why I've color-coded my friendships into four tiers based on reciprocal text message response times and birthday gift expenditure.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Because that's what love is—metrics.

jokes.text: Bert Macklin may be dead, but I'm his brother Kip Hackman. / Why wouldn't you have his same last name? / Shut up, Kyle.
jokes.setup: Bert Macklin is dead, but the bit must go on.
jokes.punchline: Andy invents a brother with an entirely different last name. Jerry points out the logical flaw. Andy shuts him down with 'Shut up, Kyle.'
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's best joke. Three elements working in perfect harmony: (1) Andy's completely illogical solution to Bert's death — same actor, different last name — delivered with total confidence; (2) Jerry actually being useful for once by pointing out the obvious flaw; (3) Andy dismissing Jerry's correct observation with 'Shut up, Kyle' — using the wrong name gag to shut down legitimate criticism. The structure is flawless. This is the rare Parks and Rec moment that approaches the anchor examples in quality. Every word earns its place.

dialogue.speaker: The Douche
dialogue.line: So I'm listening to the radio last night, right? And I hear this story about two women in the park at night, and I'm thinking, 'Oh, this is gonna be good.'

dialogue.speaker: Crazy Ira
dialogue.line: What happened?

dialogue.speaker: The Douche
dialogue.line: So the cops show up, and one of the women is all 'We were just doing government work!' And I'm like, sure you were. Government work. At night. In the park.

dialogue.speaker: The Douche
dialogue.line: Then the other one starts crying, and I'm thinking this is definitely not about government work anymore.

dialogue.speaker: Crazy Ira
dialogue.line: So what were they doing?

dialogue.speaker: The Douche
dialogue.line: I don't know, man. But whatever it was, they were really committed to their story about 'permits' and 'regulations.'

jokes.text: I know you boosted those paintings. Maybe it was me, but I'll never tell you where they are. And you'll never have my body either.
jokes.setup: Kip Hackman/Andy confronts Janet Snakehole about stolen paintings.
jokes.punchline: Janet both admits and denies the theft in the same breath ('Maybe it was me') before adding a completely non-sequitur refusal to give up her body.
jokes.explanation: 'Maybe it was me' as a confession/non-confession is a wonderfully absurd non-answer. April's commitment to melodrama with 'you'll never have my body either' — an offer no one made — is peak Janet Snakehole. April's improvisational instincts are sharp throughout this bit.

dialogue.speaker: The Douche
dialogue.line: Crazy Ira, you won't believe what happened at the club last night. This girl came up to me and said, 'You're really attractive.' So I said, 'Thanks, baby,' and she walked away. Then another girl did the same thing. I'm telling you, I was killing it out there.

dialogue.speaker: Crazy Ira
dialogue.line: Douche, those girls were hitting on you?

dialogue.speaker: The Douche
dialogue.line: Absolutely. I mean, what else could it be? Women only say things like that when they're attracted to you. It's basic biology. They were probably fighting over who got to take me home.

jokes.text: Sorry to hear the news, Tom. We're gonna miss you around the club. / Hey, you own shares, too. Why didn't Chris make you sell? / 'Cause Chris doesn't know. / You know what? Snitches get stitches.
jokes.setup: Tom learns he has to sell his shares in the Snakehole Lounge.
jokes.punchline: Donna reveals she also owns shares — Chris doesn't know — and when Tom threatens to tell, she deploys 'snitches get stitches' with total casualness.
jokes.explanation: Donna's casual threat is perfectly in character. 'Snitches get stitches' from a government employee to her colleague is funny in context and delivered with total confidence. Good Donna moment.

jokes.text: I'm a natural moneymaker. I got into government for the connections. This was supposed to be a thing that led to the other thing. It's like when Vin did Boiler Room. That's what led to him being xXx and doing Furious.
jokes.setup: Tom reflects on his career trajectory after losing his club shares.
jokes.punchline: Tom's career philosophy is apparently modeled on Vin Diesel's filmography — Boiler Room → xXx → Fast and Furious as a template for moving up.
jokes.explanation: A great Tom Haverford character joke. His earnest use of Vin Diesel's career as a blueprint for his own professional ambitions is both absurd and perfectly in character. The specificity of naming the three films makes it funnier.

jokes.text: Why don't you turn that 'frizz-own' 'upside-dizzity'?
jokes.setup: Tom encourages someone to think positively.
jokes.punchline: His version of 'turn that frown upside down' is rendered in incomprehensible slang: 'frizz-own' and 'upside-dizzity.'
jokes.explanation: Tom applying '-izzle' dialect to a cliché motivational phrase is a smart wordplay bit. 'Upside-dizzity' is genuinely inventive. Short and punchy.

jokes.text: You're wearing snow pants. / I got home last night, and I thought I might go sledding.
jokes.setup: Chris notices Ben's unusual work attire the morning after the Snake Juice disaster.
jokes.punchline: Ben's explanation — he thought he might go sledding — reveals the depth of his hangover-induced poor decision-making.
jokes.explanation: Beautifully economical. 'I thought I might go sledding' explains nothing and everything about his state of mind. The specificity of the wrong decision (sledding, not just 'warm pants') makes it funnier. Great structure.

jokes.text: Ben visits Ann at her house: Leslie doesn't know he's there. Ann: 'Oh, God. So high school.'
jokes.setup: Ben shows up at Ann's to check in on her/Leslie situation.
jokes.punchline: Ann immediately clocks it as 'so high school' — both the secret visit and the situation between Leslie and Ben.
jokes.explanation: A functional observational beat. Works because it's accurate — the whole Ben/Leslie dynamic is being conducted with teenage-level indirection. Not a standout joke but lands.

jokes.text: All I know is Leslie's always talking about how lucky she is to have you as a friend. And I just wanted you to know that.
jokes.setup: Ben has sneaked over to talk to Ann about his feelings for Leslie.
jokes.punchline: His genuine and sweet message is immediately undercut by Ann's 'You're nice.' and the dawning awareness of the romantic subtext.
jokes.explanation: More sweet than funny, but the awkward subtext earns a mild comedy credit. Ben's attempt at a casual message hiding obvious romantic interest is cringe-adjacent.

jokes.text: Oh, God. This is so high school. / Just rent a limo, ask her to the prom. I'm sure she'll say yes.
jokes.setup: Ann realizes Ben has come to talk about Leslie and makes the implicit romantic subtext explicit.
jokes.punchline: Ann's advice — rent a limo, ask her to prom — condenses her exasperation with their mutual pining into an absurd but apt teenage romance metaphor.
jokes.explanation: Ann's exasperated-friend energy is well-deployed. The prom metaphor is apt and the delivery sells it.

jokes.text: So let me get this straight. Tom tries to get off the government teat, and we punish him. That doesn't make any sense to me.
jokes.setup: The group discusses Tom being forced to sell his club shares.
jokes.punchline: Ron frames Chris's enforcement of ethics rules as 'punishing' Tom for private enterprise — perfectly in line with his anti-government philosophy.
jokes.explanation: Ron's libertarian perspective applied to a workplace ethics violation is consistently funny. 'The government teat' is vivid and in character. His genuine bafflement at ethics enforcement is perfect Ron Swanson.

jokes.text: Leslie's defense of Tom to Chris: 'He's not savvy enough to manipulate the system like that. He's just a kid chasing a goofy dream.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is making a case for Tom to Chris — defending him from the accusation of corruption.
jokes.punchline: Her defense is 'He's not savvy enough to manipulate the system' — an inadvertent insult that's also the most effective argument she has.
jokes.explanation: Leslie's passionate defense inadvertently demolishing Tom's intelligence is a perfect character joke. She's 100% sincere and 100% right, and the compliment-insult combination ('just a kid chasing a goofy dream') is both sweet and cutting. Strong character integration — this is quintessential Leslie defending her friends.

jokes.text: Jan Cooper was a terrible wife. I just want everybody to know that. / Thank you, Dennis. But we can't give you your job back. / You sound just like her.
jokes.setup: Dennis Cooper, the fired PR Director who plastered City Hall with Chlamydia signs, appears at the interview process.
jokes.punchline: His final statement — 'you sound just like her' directed at Ben for refusing to give him his job back — suggests his wife also reasonably refused him things.
jokes.explanation: A great callback to the episode's opening scandal. 'You sound just like her' directed at Ben for professional behavior implies Jan's 'no' was equally reasonable. The line recontextualizes Dennis as the actual problem in the marriage.

jokes.text: Your sweater's on inside out. / And backwards. / It's been a tough morning. / Lots of regret and shame. That should be the official slogan for Snake Juice.
jokes.setup: Ann shows up for her second interview, visibly disheveled from the night before.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's deadpan assessment of Ann's sweater situation, followed by 'lots of regret and shame' — then immediately proposing it as Snake Juice's marketing slogan.
jokes.explanation: 'Lots of regret and shame — that should be the official slogan for Snake Juice' is one of the best lines in the episode. It's a perfect encapsulation of the evening, a great product joke, and delivered in a moment of genuine friendship reconciliation. The economy is excellent.

jokes.text: This committee would like to ask if you are the kind of candidate who could forgive someone after they've behaved like a complete jackass? / This candidate could, especially because this candidate also behaved like a total jackass.
jokes.setup: Leslie and Ann's reconciliation is conducted entirely through the formal language of a job interview.
jokes.punchline: Both apologies are phrased in third-person 'this committee/this candidate' HR interview language — an absurd formal register for a deeply personal conversation.
jokes.explanation: A genuinely clever structural joke: the interview format provides cover for genuine emotional expression. 'This committee' and 'this candidate' used for a personal apology is both funny and warm. It works as comedy AND character development simultaneously. High craft score justified.

jokes.text: Also, I can talk about my qualifications for this position. But first, I am gonna go throw up in a wastebasket.
jokes.setup: Ann's interview/reconciliation scene concludes.
jokes.punchline: She professionally notes she can discuss qualifications but must first vomit — stated with complete composure.
jokes.explanation: The professionalism of the delivery against the content is the joke. Placing vomiting on the agenda before qualifications, calmly, is a good hangover comedy beat.

jokes.text: Would you mind if I joined you? / Not at all. / Shall we?
jokes.setup: Ann announces she must throw up in a wastebasket.
jokes.punchline: Leslie formally requests to join her. They exit together to vomit, with 'Shall we?' as a refined invitation.
jokes.explanation: 'Shall we?' as a refined invitation to go vomit together is a perfect button on the reconciliation scene. It's also a great distillation of Leslie and Ann's friendship — even mutual vomiting is approached with warmth and formality. The economy is excellent.

jokes.text: We need to remember what's important in life. Friends, waffles, and work. Or waffles, friends, work. It doesn't matter. But work is third.
jokes.setup: Leslie reflects on the lessons of the episode.
jokes.punchline: Her wisdom is immediately complicated by uncertainty about whether friends or waffles come first — but work is definitively third.
jokes.explanation: One of the most quotable Leslie Knope lines ever written. The joke is that she's unsure whether friends or waffles come first but is completely certain work is third. Her love of waffles being elevated to friend-level priority is perfect character comedy. The hedging ('or waffles, friends, work. It doesn't matter.') then the certainty ('But work is third') is perfectly structured. High score justified.

jokes.text: So I'm dancing on the floor with this super-hot chick. / Me so horny. / More like a dude, I bet. / Hello? / Did you wet your whistle? / I wish. / Me likey.
jokes.setup: The Douche recounts his night at the Snakehole on his radio show.
jokes.punchline: His co-host Crazy Ira's running commentary ('More like a dude, I bet,' 'Me likey') frames the entire episode's events through the lens of the worst morning radio imaginable.
jokes.explanation: The recontextualization of the episode's events as trash radio content is a clever structural device. Crazy Ira's commentary is deliberately awful, which is the joke. Works as a coda.

jokes.text: No, no, no, no. She spent the whole night talking to her friend, arguing about their feelings. / That's me! / Who knows? She's probably a lesbian. / They were in the bathroom a long time.
jokes.setup: The Douche describes Leslie and Ann's fight as his reason for not hooking up. Leslie hears herself described on the radio.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's 'That's me!' realization — hearing herself described reductively on a shock radio show — then Crazy Ira's reflexive 'she's probably a lesbian' followed by the bathroom observation.
jokes.explanation: A strong episode-closing structural joke. Leslie recognizing herself on the radio while the hosts reduce her friendship with Ann to a punchline is both funny and appropriately deflating. The mockumentary-style awareness of being seen is well-used.

tmdb_overview: When Leslie tries to get Ann a job at city hall, her lukewarm reaction causes their first-ever fight. Tom invites the entire department to the Snakehole Lounge to help him promote his new alcohol, "Snake Juice."
insight: Escalation-driven character comedy sustains 62 jokes across tense group dynamics with minimal setup.
